::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Four things a load cell calibration has to separate {#sec-m1-loadcell}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Four things a load cell calibration has to separate (1)
:::

A load cell is a strain-gauge bridge bonded inside a metal body shaped so
that a known force $F$ produces a repeatable bridge output. "Repeatable" is
doing a lot of work in that sentence, and static calibration against
reference masses is where you find out how much:

- **Linearity.** Fit a straight line $V = a + bF$ to the indication against
  the applied force and look at the residuals. Report **non-linearity** as
  the largest residual expressed as a percentage of the full-scale output,
  $$
  \mathrm{NL} = \frac{\max_i \lvert V_i - (a+bF_i)\rvert}{V_\mathrm{FS}}\times 100\,\%
  $$ {#eq-m1-linearity}
  exactly the same construction as [S1's calibration
  residual](../S1-daq-static/handbook.qmd#sec-s1-calibration), now against a
  mechanical reference instead of a voltage one.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Four things a load cell calibration has to separate (2)
:::

- **Hysteresis.** Load the cell up through a sequence of masses, then unload
  through the same sequence in reverse, and compare the two readings at each
  nominal force:
  $$
  \mathrm{H} = \frac{\max_i \lvert V_\mathrm{loading}(F_i) -
  V_\mathrm{unloading}(F_i)\rvert}{V_\mathrm{FS}}\times 100\,\%
  $$ {#eq-m1-hysteresis}
  Unlike non-linearity, hysteresis cannot be removed by a better fit: it is a
  path dependence, not a curvature, and it sets a floor under how well any
  single calibration curve can predict either direction of loading.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Four things a load cell calibration has to separate (3)
:::

- **Creep.** Hold one mass constant and keep recording. A bridge bonded with
  an imperfect adhesive, or a body with viscoelastic behaviour under
  sustained stress, drifts even though $F$ has not changed. A single
  exponential is the usual first model,
  $$
  V(t) = V(0)\left[1 + C_\infty\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)\right]
  $$ {#eq-m1-creep}
  with $C_\infty$ the fractional drift as $t\to\infty$ and $\tau$ a time
  constant; fitting @eq-m1-creep to a long hold is what turns "the reading
  seems to wander" into a number you can put a bound on.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Four things a load cell calibration has to separate (4)
:::

- **Zero drift.** Return to zero force and compare the reading with the zero
  you started from. Because @eq-m1-hysteresis is built to close to zero at
  both ends of the sweep by construction (loading and unloading agree at
  $F=0$ and at $F=F_\mathrm{cap}$), a non-zero difference between the
  *first* zero of the session and the *last* one — taken after the whole
  loading/unloading/creep sequence — is evidence of something else: thermal
  drift of the bridge or the amplifier, not the hysteresis loop.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Why the instrumentation amplifier is not optional {#sec-m1-inamp}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Why the instrumentation amplifier is not optional (1)
:::

A quarter bridge with gauge factor $k$ at strain $\varepsilon$, excited at
$V_\mathrm{ex}$, produces a differential output
$$
\frac{\Delta V}{V_\mathrm{ex}} = \frac{k\varepsilon}{4}
$$ {#eq-m1-quarter}
— see [Strain gauge technology](../../hardware/beam-rig.qmd) [@window] for
the derivation from the four-arm bridge equation. Work through what that is
in volts. Taking the reference data's own placeholders (see
`tools/synth/params/m1.yaml`) of $k = 2.1$ and $V_\mathrm{ex} = 5$ V, at a
representative strain $\varepsilon = 10^{-4}$ — a typical order of magnitude
for an elastic metal structure well inside yield —
$$
\Delta V = \frac{k\varepsilon V_\mathrm{ex}}{4}
        = \frac{2.1 \times 10^{-4} \times 5}{4}\ \mathrm{V}
        \approx 0.26\ \mathrm{mV}
$$ {#eq-m1-quarter-numeric}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Why the instrumentation amplifier is not optional (2)
:::

Compare that with [S1](../S1-daq-static/handbook.qmd#sec-s1-enob): on this
same board's ADC, one LSB is about $50\ \mu$V and the measured noise floor is
of the order of $0.5$ mV RMS. @eq-m1-quarter-numeric is a handful of LSB —
comparable to a single sample of S1's own noise — before the signal has
travelled any further than the gauge leads. Unamplified, the bridge signal is
not distinguishable from the converter's own noise; this is arithmetic, not
an assumption, and it is the reason every strain-gauge measurement on this
site goes through an instrumentation amplifier before the ADC (see [the
conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd#sec-cond-inamp) for
why an in-amp specifically, rather than a single op-amp, is the right part:
CMRR against a bridge sitting at several volts of common mode).

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Why the instrumentation amplifier is not optional (3)
:::

**Sizing the gain.** Design the amplifier so a chosen full-scale strain
$\varepsilon_\mathrm{fs}$ drives the ADC input to $V_\mathrm{hi}$, leaving the
same kind of headroom as [S3's conditioning
stage](../S3-aliasing-filtering/handbook.qmd#sec-s3-conditioning) —
$[p_\mathrm{lo}, p_\mathrm{hi}]$ of $V_\mathrm{ref}$, not the full rail:
$$
G = \frac{(p_\mathrm{hi}-p_\mathrm{lo})\,V_\mathrm{ref}}
       {k\,\varepsilon_\mathrm{fs}\,V_\mathrm{ex}/4}
$$ {#eq-m1-required-gain}
With $\varepsilon_\mathrm{fs} = 10^{-4}$ (the same strain used above,
now doing double duty as the design target), $p_\mathrm{lo}=0.05$,
$p_\mathrm{hi}=0.95$ and $V_\mathrm{ref}=3.3$ V, @eq-m1-required-gain gives
$G \approx 1.13\times 10^4$ — a gain in the tens of thousands, not tens, is
what a bare micro-strain signal needs; the reference generator uses exactly
this value (`tools/synth/m1_strain_load.py` computes it from
`tools/synth/params/m1.yaml` at generation time, so the theory and the
reference data never disagree).

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### On the beam: quarter, half and full bridge {#sec-m1-bridges}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### On the beam: quarter, half and full bridge (1)
:::

A single active gauge (quarter bridge) gives @eq-m1-quarter. Replacing one of
the bridge's fixed resistors with a second active gauge (half bridge), or all
four arms with active gauges (full bridge), multiplies the sensitivity:
$$
\frac{\Delta V}{V_\mathrm{ex}} =
\begin{cases}
k\varepsilon/4 & \text{quarter bridge (1 active arm)} \\
k\varepsilon/2 & \text{half bridge (2 active arms)} \\
k\varepsilon   & \text{full bridge (4 active arms)}
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-m1-bridge-configs}

Which arrangement is used is a decision about what you want to cancel, not
just about sensitivity:

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### On the beam: quarter, half and full bridge (2)
:::

- **Quarter bridge**, one gauge at the strain-gauge position, is sensitive to
  bending strain but also to the gauge's own temperature coefficient (its
  resistance drifts with temperature regardless of load) and to axial load
  superimposed on bending.
- **Half bridge**, one active gauge at the measurement position and one
  *dummy* gauge bonded to an unstrained piece of the same material (same
  thermal environment, no mechanical strain), placed in an adjacent bridge
  arm so their temperature-driven resistance changes cancel in the bridge
  equation while their strain response does not. This is [the temperature
  compensation](#sec-m1-temp) below.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### On the beam: quarter, half and full bridge (3)
:::

- **Half bridge, both gauges on the beam** (one on the top surface, one on
  the bottom, at the same $x$) instead cancels axial load — which produces
  equal-sign strain on both surfaces — while doubling the bending-strain
  signal, since bending produces opposite-sign strain top and bottom. This is
  a different half-bridge wiring from the dummy-gauge one above, and the two
  should not be confused: one cancels temperature, the other cancels axial
  load, and neither does both.
- **Full bridge**, four active gauges (two on each surface, at the root),
  cancels both temperature and axial load simultaneously, at the cost of two
  more gauges to bond and wire.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Temperature compensation, measured rather than assumed {#sec-m1-temp}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Temperature compensation, measured rather than assumed (1)
:::

A bare quarter bridge cannot tell a real mechanical strain from an apparent
one produced by the gauge's own resistance changing with temperature. Design
the test directly: change the beam's temperature by a known amount with the
beam **unloaded** ($F=0$), and record both a quarter bridge and a
dummy-compensated half bridge. Any output that appears is, by construction,
entirely apparent strain — there is no real mechanical strain to confuse it
with — so
$$
\alpha_\mathrm{apparent} = \frac{1}{\Delta T}\times
  \frac{4\,\Delta V/V_\mathrm{ex}}{n_\mathrm{arm}\,k}
$$ {#eq-m1-temp-apparent}
gives the apparent strain per kelvin directly from the measured $\Delta V$,
with $n_\mathrm{arm}=1$ for the quarter bridge and $2$ for the half bridge.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Temperature compensation, measured rather than assumed (2)
:::

A half bridge does not cancel the effect to zero — the dummy gauge's own
temperature coefficient only matches the active gauge's to within
manufacturing tolerance — but $\alpha_\mathrm{apparent}$ for the half bridge
should be a small fraction of the quarter bridge's value, and the ratio
between the two is the compensation's own figure of merit.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Nothing here depends on the beam's length, width or thickness: the test is
done at $F=0$, so no bending strain is involved, and @eq-m1-temp-apparent
converts a measured voltage directly into an apparent strain using only the
gauge factor and the bridge arm count — both properties of the sensing
chain, not of the beam.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Choosing the measurand for the budget {#sec-m1-budget-choice}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Choosing the measurand for the budget (1)
:::

M1 measures two different things — a load-cell voltage calibrated against a
force, and a beam-mounted bridge's strain — and a single uncertainty budget
has to pick one. This handbook budgets the **beam-mounted quarter bridge's
strain**, $\hat\varepsilon$, because it is the quantity
[M2](../M2-hall-displacement/index.qmd) needs for the stiffness cross-check,
and because its budget exercises every component this experiment
introduces: the gauge factor's own tolerance, the amplifier's gain and
offset, the reference masses, and [S1's effective
quantization](../S1-daq-static/handbook.qmd#sec-s1-enob). Inverting
@eq-m1-quarter for a measured $\Delta V$,
$$
\hat\varepsilon = \frac{4\,\Delta V}{k\,V_\mathrm{ex}}
$$ {#eq-m1-strain-recover}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Choosing the measurand for the budget (2)
:::

with sensitivity coefficients
$$
\frac{\partial\hat\varepsilon}{\partial \Delta V} = \frac{4}{kV_\mathrm{ex}},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\hat\varepsilon}{\partial k} = -\frac{\hat\varepsilon}{k},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\hat\varepsilon}{\partial V_\mathrm{ex}} = -\frac{\hat\varepsilon}{V_\mathrm{ex}}
$$ {#eq-m1-sensitivity}
The load-cell's own hysteresis (@eq-m1-hysteresis) enters the strain budget
as a bound on the amplifier chain shared by both sensors, following [the
conditioning board's uncertainty
treatment](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd#sec-cond-budget).

### Relation to S1 {#sec-m1-relation}

Every number in @eq-m1-quarter-numeric and @eq-m1-required-gain is only
useful because [S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) already measured what the
ADC alone can resolve. M1 does not re-measure the converter; it reads S1's
noise floor and effective quantization off the shelf and asks what gain
makes a real bridge signal usable against them — the same relationship [S3
has with S1](../S3-aliasing-filtering/handbook.qmd#sec-s3-relation), now for
a mechanical rather than a generated electrical signal.
